details:
**Hall–Héroult process**
The main industrial method for making aluminum metal. Alumina (aluminum oxide) is dissolved in molten cryolite and electrolyzed, using carbon anodes that are either prebaked or of the Söderberg type. Charles Martin Hall in the US and Paul Héroult in France developed it independently and patented it almost at the same time in 1886.

**Bayer process**
The process that refines bauxite into pure alumina. The ground ore is digested in hot sodium hydroxide, which dissolves the aluminum compounds but not the iron oxides. Aluminum hydroxide is then precipitated and heated to give alumina. Gallium is recovered as a byproduct, and the process replaced the earlier Deville process.

**Bauxite**
The main ore of aluminum, a rock made of the aluminum hydroxide minerals gibbsite, boehmite, and diaspore. It is also a source of gallium.

**Cryolite (Na3AlF6)**
Sodium hexafluoroaluminate, a mineral made of three sodium atoms, one aluminum atom, and six fluorine atoms. In the Hall–Héroult process it is the molten solvent for alumina, lowering the melting point. For many years most natural cryolite came from a single deposit at Ivigtut in Greenland; today it is mostly synthetic.

**Corundum (aluminum oxide)**
Crystalline Al2O3, which defines hardness 9 on the Mohs scale and is used as an abrasive (emery). Chromium impurities make it red, as ruby; other impurities give sapphire. Synthetic rubies and sapphires are made from powdered alumina by the Verneuil flame-fusion process.

**Lithium aluminum hydride (LiAlH4)**
A powerful reducing agent in organic chemistry, stronger than sodium borohydride. It reduces aldehydes, ketones, esters, and carboxylic acids to alcohols.

**Aluminum chloride and Friedel–Crafts reactions**
Aluminum trichloride is a strong Lewis acid because aluminum, like its group-mate boron, is trivalent and electron-deficient. It is the classic catalyst for Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation of aromatic rings. Iron(III) halides do the same job.

**Most abundant metal in Earth's crust**
Aluminum makes up about 8% of the crust by weight, more than any other metal (only oxygen and silicon are more abundant overall). It occurs in all feldspars, in clays such as kaolinite, and in many other silicate minerals.

**Soda cans and foil**
The most familiar uses of aluminum, which is light, malleable, and corrosion-resistant. Aluminum foil replaced the older tin foil, though people still call it "tin foil." The metal is also used in aircraft hulls and vehicles.

**Zeolites**
Microporous aluminosilicate minerals in which aluminum and silicon atoms are linked through oxygen. They are used as adsorbents, molecular sieves, ion exchangers, and catalysts.

**Alums and aluminum sulfate as flocculants**
Alums are double salts of aluminum sulfate with a group 1 metal sulfate, such as potassium alum, KAl(SO4)2·12H2O. Alum and aluminum sulfate make tiny particles clump together, so they are used in water purification, papermaking, and as fire retardants.

**Calcium–aluminum-rich inclusions (CAIs) and aluminum-26**
CAIs found in chondritic meteorites are the oldest known solids in the solar system and are used to date it. Aluminum-26 is a radioactive isotope that decays to magnesium-26; on Earth it forms when cosmic rays strike argon in the atmosphere.

**Raney nickel**
A porous nickel catalyst used for hydrogenation. It is made by alloying nickel with aluminum and then leaching the aluminum out with sodium hydroxide.

**Passivation and anodizing**
Aluminum resists corrosion because a thin, transparent oxide layer forms on its surface. Anodizing thickens this layer electrochemically. Mercury breaks through the layer and amalgamates with aluminum, which is why airlines restrict mercury barometers.

**Washington Monument capstone and early isolation**
Before the Hall–Héroult process, aluminum was more valuable than silver, so in 1884 it was chosen for the capstone of the Washington Monument. Hans Christian Ørsted first isolated it in 1825 using potassium amalgam, and Friedrich Wöhler improved the method by reducing aluminum chloride with potassium.
